x: Commentary on the Surah “When the Sky Is Split Open”
In the name of God, the Most Compassionate, the Most Merciful.
The explanation of the interpretation of the saying of the Exalted: “When the sky is split open
n
, when the stars are scattered
n
, when the seas are made to burst forth
n
, when the graves are overturned (4), a soul will know what it has sent ahead and what it has left behind (5).”

God, exalted is His mention, says: “When the sky is split open,” meaning: when it is cleft apart; and when its stars are scattered out of it and fall. “And when the seas are made to burst forth”: He says that God causes some of them to flow into others, so that they all become filled.
The people of interpretation expressed views similar to what we have said, although they differed concerning some details.
Those who said this include the following:

m: he said: Abu Salih narrated to us; he said: Mu'awiyah narrated to me, from Ali, from Ibn Abbas, concerning His saying, “And when the seas are made to burst forth.” He said: Some of them flow into others (1).

he said: Yazid narrated to us; he said: Sa'id narrated to us, from Qatadah, concerning His saying, “And when the seas are made to burst forth”: Their fresh water is poured into their salt water, and their salt water into their fresh water (2).

c: Ibn Abd al-A'la narrated to us;
m: he said: Ibn Thawr narrated to us, from Ma'mar (3), from al-Hasan, concerning “And when the seas are made to burst forth...” “...and when the seas are made to burst forth.” He said: Some of them flow into others, and their water disappears
n
. Al-Kalbi said: They are filled
n

x: And His saying: “And when the graves are overturned.” He says: When the graves are stirred up and those of the dead who are inside them are brought out alive. In Arabic, one says, “So-and-so ba'thara the basin of so-and-so,” when he turns its bottom upward.
i
Ba'thara
and
i
baḥthara
are two dialectal forms.
The people of interpretation expressed a view similar to what we have said.
Those who said this include the following:

m: he said: Abu Salih narrated to us; he said: Mu'awiyah narrated to me, from Ali, from Ibn Abbas, concerning His saying, “And when the graves are overturned.” He said: They are dug up
n

x: And His saying: “A soul will know what it has sent ahead and what it has left behind.” God, exalted is His mention, says: Every
n
soul will know what righteous deed it sent ahead for that Day, from which it will benefit, and what it left behind of something it instituted as a practice that is followed
n
The people of interpretation differed over how this is to be understood.
Some of them held a view similar to what we have stated.
Those who said this include the following:

c: Ibn Abd al-A'la narrated to us;
m: he said: al-Mu'tamir ibn Sulayman narrated to us, from his father, who said: I was told, from al-Qurazi, that he said concerning “A soul will know what it has sent ahead and what it has left behind”: “What it sent ahead” is what it did; as for “what it left behind,” it is a practice that a person establishes and that is followed after him
n

x: Others said that this refers to the obligatory duties that a person performed among what he sent ahead, and the obligatory duties that he neglected among what he left behind.
Those who said this include the following:

m: he said: Waki' narrated to us, from his father, from Sa'id ibn Masruq, from Ikrimah, concerning “A soul will know what it has sent ahead.” He said: The duties imposed upon it, and what it delayed. He meant the duties imposed upon it
n

c: Muhammad ibn Sa'd narrated to me;
m: he said: My father narrated to me; he said: My uncle narrated to me; he said: My father narrated to me, from his father, from Ibn Abbas, concerning His saying, “A soul will know what it has sent ahead and what it has left behind.” He said: It will know what it sent ahead of obedience to God and what it left undone of what it had been commanded
n

he said: Yazid narrated to us; he said: Sa'id narrated to us, from Qatadah, concerning His saying, “A soul will know what it has sent ahead and what it has left behind.” He said: What it sent ahead of good, and what it left undone of God's due upon it
n

c: Ibn Abd al-A'la narrated to us;
m: he said: Ibn Thawr narrated to us, from Ma'mar, from Qatadah, concerning “what it has sent ahead...” “...and what it has left behind.” He said: What it sent ahead of obedience to God, and what it left undone of God's due
n

he said: Ibn Wahb informed us; he said: Ibn Zayd said concerning His saying, “A soul will know what it has sent ahead and what it has left behind”: What it sent ahead is what it did; what it left behind is what it abandoned and neglected, including the righteous deeds to which God had called it.

x: Others said: Rather, the meaning is whatever good or evil it sent ahead, and whatever good or evil it left behind.
Those who said this include the following:

m: he said: Hushaym narrated to us; he said: al-'Awwam informed us, from Ibrahim al-Taymi, who said—when this verse, “A soul will know what it has sent ahead and what it has left behind,” was mentioned in his presence—“I am among what al-Hajjaj has left behind.”

x: We have chosen the interpretation we stated because every good or evil deed a servant performs is something he has sent ahead. Whatever of God's due upon him he neglects and falls short in performing is likewise something evil that he has sent ahead. It is not something he has left behind in the sense of a deed, because a deed is what a person has actually done. As for what he has not done, it is only an evil that he has sent ahead. Therefore, we have said that “what he left behind” is a good or bad practice that he established, such that whoever acts upon it receives a reward like that of the person who acted upon it, or bears a burden like his.
The explanation of the interpretation of the saying of the Exalted: “O human being!

What has deceived you concerning your Generous Lord (6), who created you, fashioned you, and proportioned you (7), assembling you in whatever form He wished (8)?” He, exalted is His mention, says: “O disbelieving human being! What has deceived you concerning your Generous Lord?” The enemy appointed over the human being—Satan—has deceived people concerning Him
n

m: he said: Yazid narrated to us; he said: Sa'id narrated to us, from Qatadah, concerning “What has deceived you concerning your Generous Lord?” He said: What has deceived the son of Adam? This enemy, Satan
n

x: And His saying: “Who created you and fashioned you.” He says: He created you, O human being, fashioned your creation, and proportioned you.
The reciters differed in how they recited this. The majority of the reciters of Medina, Mecca, Syria, and Basra recited it as
i
fa-'addalaka
, with a doubled dal
n
. The majority of the reciters of Kufa recited it with a light, undoubled dal
n

Those who recited it with a doubled consonant appear to have understood the meaning as: He made you balanced, proportionate in bodily constitution, and upright. Those who recited it without doubling appear to have understood the meaning as: He turned and directed you toward whatever form He wished—whether a beautiful form, an ugly form, or the form of one of your relatives
n
In my view, the soundest position is to say
n

that these are two well-known readings among the regional reciters, and both have sound meanings. Whichever one a reciter uses, he is correct. However, the reading I find preferable is that of those who pronounce the dal with doubling, because the use of the preposition “in” to express proportioning is more idiomatic in Arabic than its use to express turning or directing. The explanation of this continues on the following page. ...Arabic, when used to express proportioning, than when used to express turning or directing. Do you not see that you say, “I proportioned you in such-and-such,” and “I turned you toward it,” whereas you hardly say, “I proportioned you toward such-and-such,” or “I turned you in it”? For this reason I preferred the doubled form.
Reports from the people of interpretation express the meaning in the way we have stated, and indicate that the reciters understood it as we have described.
The reports concerning this are as follows:

c: Muhammad ibn Amr narrated to me;
m: he said: Abu Asim narrated to us; he said: Isa narrated to us.

he said: al-Hasan narrated to us; he said: Waraq narrated to us. Both routes go from Ibn Abi Najih, from Mujahid, concerning God's saying, “In whatever form He wished, He assembled you (8).” He said: In whatever likeness—of a father, mother, maternal uncle, or paternal uncle
n
he said: Waki' narrated to us, from Sufyan, from Isma'il
n
, concerning His saying, “He assembled you as He wished.” He said: If He wished, in the form of a dog; and if He wished, in the form of a donkey.
he said: Mihran narrated to us, from Sufyan, from Isma'il, from Abu Salih, concerning “In whatever form He wished, He assembled you (8).” He said: A pig or a donkey
n

he said: Ibn 'Ulayyah narrated to us, from Abu Raja', from Ikrimah, concerning His saying, “In whatever form He wished, He assembled you (8).” He said: If He wished, in the form of a monkey; and if He wished, in the form of a pig
n

c: Muhammad ibn Sinan al-Qazzaz narrated to me;
m: he said: Mutahhar ibn al-Haytham narrated to us; he said: Musa ibn Ali ibn
n
Rabbah al-Lakhmi narrated to us; he said: My father narrated to me, from my grandfather, that the Prophet—God bless him and grant him peace—said to him: “What has been born to you
n

x: He replied: “Messenger of God, what could be born to me? Either a boy or a girl.”
He asked: “And whom will the child resemble?”
He replied: “Messenger of God, whom could the child resemble except its father or its mother?”

The Prophet then said: “Stop! Do not say that. When the drop settles in the womb, God brings together every lineage between it and Adam. Have you not read this verse in the Book of God: ‘In whatever form He wished, He assembled you (8)’?”
He said: “He traced your lineage”
n

evidence.text: The reciters differed in how they recited this.
The majority of the reciters of Medina, Mecca, Syria, and Basra recited it as *fa-'addalaka*, with a doubled dal (3).
The majority of the reciters of Kufa recited it with a light, undoubled dal (4).
Those who recited it with a doubled consonant appear to have understood the meaning as: He made you balanced, proportionate in bodily constitution, and upright.

Those who recited it without doubling appear to have understood the meaning as: He turned and directed you toward whatever form He wished—whether a beautiful form, an ugly form, or the form of one of your relatives (5).
In my view, the soundest position is to say (6) that these are two well-known readings among the regional reciters, and both have sound meanings.

However, the reading I find preferable is that of those who pronounce the dal with doubling, because the use of the preposition “in” to express proportioning is more idiomatic in Arabic than its use to express turning or directing.
Reports from the people of interpretation express the meaning in the way we have stated, and indicate that the reciters understood it as we have described.
Have you not read this verse in the Book of God: ‘In whatever form He wished, He assembled you (8)’?”

x: The explanation of the interpretation of the saying of the Exalted: “No indeed!
Rather, you deny the Recompense (9), while over you are guardians (10), noble scribes (11), who know what you do (12). Surely, the righteous will be in bliss (13).”

God, exalted is His mention, says: The matter is not as you disbelievers claim—that you are upon the truth in worshipping other than God. Rather, you deny reward and punishment, recompense and reckoning.
The people of interpretation expressed a meaning similar to what we have stated concerning His saying, “No indeed! Rather, you deny the Recompense (9).”
Those who said this include the following:

c: Muhammad ibn Amr narrated to me;
m: he said: Abu Asim narrated to us; he said: Isa narrated to us.
he said: al-Hasan narrated to us; he said: Waraq narrated to us. Both routes go from Ibn Abi Najih, from Mujahid, concerning His saying, “Rather, you deny the Recompense (9).” He said: The reckoning.
he said: al-Hasan narrated to us; he said: Waraq narrated to us. Both routes go from Ibn Abi Najih, from Mujahid, concerning “Rather, you deny the Recompense (9).” He said: The Day of Reckoning
n

c: Ibn Abd al-A'la narrated to us;
m: he said: Ibn Thawr narrated to us, from Ma'mar, from Qatadah, concerning His saying, “Rather, you deny the Recompense.” He said: A day of severity, a day on which God requites the servants for their deeds
n

x: And His saying: “And over you are guardians (10).” He says: Over you are watchers who guard your deeds and enumerate them against you.
“Noble scribes (11).” He says: Honored by God; “scribes” means that they write down your deeds.
The people of interpretation expressed a meaning similar to what we have stated.
Those who said this include the following:

m: he said: Ibn 'Ulayyah narrated to us; he said: One of our companions reported from Ayyub, concerning His saying, “And over you are guardians (10), noble scribes (11).” He said: They write down what you say and what you intend
n

x: And His saying: “They know what you do (12).” He says: These guardians know whatever good or evil you do, and they record it against you.

And His saying: “Surely, the righteous will be in bliss (13).” The Exalted says: Those who acted righteously by fulfilling God's obligations and avoiding acts of disobedience will surely be in the bliss of the Gardens, where they will be given delight.
The explanation of the interpretation of the saying of the Exalted: “And surely, the wicked will be in Hellfire (14), entering it on the Day of Recompense (15).

They will not be absent from it (16). And what will make you know what the Day of Recompense is (17)? Again, what will make you know what the Day of Recompense is (18)? The Day when no soul will possess anything for another soul, and the command on that Day will belong to God (19).”
God, exalted is His mention, says: “And surely, the wicked”—those who disbelieved in their Lord—“will be in Hellfire.”

And His saying: “Entering it on the Day of Recompense (15).” The Exalted says: These wicked people will enter Hellfire on the Day of Resurrection, the day on which the servants are requited for their deeds
n
, and repaid for them.
The people of interpretation expressed a meaning similar to what we have stated.
Those who said this include the following:

m: he said: Abu Salih narrated to us; he said: Mu'awiyah narrated to me, from Ali, from Ibn Abbas, concerning His saying, “The Day of Recompense.” He said: It is one of the names of the Day of Resurrection. God has magnified it and warned His servants about it
n

x: And His saying: “They will not be absent from it (16).” God, exalted is His mention, says: These wicked people will never leave Hellfire and thus be absent from it. Rather, they will remain there forever. The righteous are likewise [permanently] in bliss. This is similar to His saying: “They will not be brought out of it (48)” [al-Hijr 15:48]. ...and they will remain in bliss. This is like His saying: “They will not be brought out of it (48)” [al-Hijr 15:48].

And His saying: “And what will make you know what the Day of Recompense is (17)?” God, exalted is His mention, says to His Prophet Muhammad—God bless him and grant him peace: “And what will make you know,” O Muhammad? That is, what will inform you “what the Day of Recompense is”—what sort of day the Day of Reckoning and repayment is? He says this to magnify its importance.
The people of interpretation expressed a meaning similar to what we have stated.
Those who said this include the following:

m: he said: Yazid narrated to us; he said: Sa'id narrated to us, from Qatadah, concerning His saying, “And what will make you know what the Day of Recompense is (17)?” He said: This is to magnify the Day of Resurrection: a day on which people will be requited for their deeds
n

x: And His saying: “Again, what will make you know what the Day of Recompense is (18)?” He says: Then what has informed you, O Muhammad, what sort of day the Day of Repayment and Reckoning is? This is to magnify its importance. Then the Exalted explained some of its features, saying: “The Day when no soul will possess anything for another soul.”

God, exalted is His mention, says: That is the day “when no soul will possess” anything. He means that no soul will be able to avail another soul in any way: it will not be able to ward off a calamity that has befallen it, nor provide it with any benefit. In this world, that soul may have protected it and defended it against anyone who sought to harm it. All of that will come to an end on that Day, because command will belong to God; no victor can overcome Him, and no conqueror can subdue Him. Kingdoms will vanish there, positions of authority will disappear, and sovereignty will belong to the Sovereign, the Compeller. This is the meaning of His saying, “And the command on that Day will belong to God.” He says: All command on that Day—that is, judgment and dominion—belongs to God alone, apart from all His other creatures. No creature will share with Him any command or prohibition on that Day.
The people of interpretation expressed a meaning similar to what we have stated.
Those who said this include the following:

c: Ibn Abd al-A'la narrated to us;
m: he said: Ibn Thawr narrated to us, from Ma'mar, from Qatadah, concerning His saying, “And the command on that Day will belong to God.” He said: On that Day, no one there will decide anything or do anything except the Lord of the Worlds
n

he said: Yazid narrated to us; he said: Sa'id narrated to us, from Qatadah, concerning His saying, “The Day when no soul will possess anything for another soul, and the command on that Day will belong to God (19).” He said: By God, command belongs to God today as well, but on that Day no one will dispute it with Him
n

x: The reciters differed in how they recited His saying, “The Day when no soul will possess...” The majority of the reciters of the Hijaz and Kufa recited “the Day” in the accusative, because the grammatical annexation is not a pure construct
n
Some of the reciters of Basra recited “the Day” in the nominative, as a continuation of the nominative form of the first occurrence of “the Day”
n

The nominative is more eloquent in Arabic usage. This is because “day” is annexed to an imperfect verb. When the Arabs annex “day” to “you do,” “he does,” or “I do,” they put it in the nominative and say, “This is the day on which I do such-and-such.” When they annex it to a past-tense verb, they put it in the accusative
n
. An example is the poet's verse
n
“At the time when I reproached old age for youth,
and said, ‘Will you not come to your senses, while grey hair restrains you?’”
End of the commentary on the Surah “When the Sky Is Split Open.”

evidence.text: The reciters differed in how they recited His saying, “The Day when no soul will possess...”
The majority of the reciters of the Hijaz and Kufa recited “the Day” in the accusative, because the grammatical annexation is not a pure construct (3).
Some of the reciters of Basra recited “the Day” in the nominative, as a continuation of the nominative form of the first occurrence of “the Day” (4).

notes.en: T3 reads “bi-aʿmalihim” (“by their deeds”).
notes.ar: في ت 3: "بأعمالهم".

notes.en: The source references were given earlier at 20/296.
notes.ar: تقدم تخريجه في 20/ 296.

notes.en: Manuscript M reads “min” (“from”).
notes.ar: في م: (من).

notes.en: The source references were given earlier at 19/518.
notes.ar: تقدم تخريجه في 19/ 518

notes.en: Manuscripts S, T1, T2, and T3 read “fa-yudfaʿu ʿanhu” (“so it is warded off from him”).
notes.ar: في ص، ت 1، ت،2، ت 3: "فيدفع عنه".

notes.en: ʿAbd al-Razzaq transmitted it in his Tafsir (2/354) from Maʿmar with this chain. Al-Suyuti attributed it in al-Durr al-Manthur (6/323) to ʿAbd ibn Humayd and Ibn al-Mundhir.
notes.ar: أخرجه عبد الرزاق في تفسيره 2/ 354 عن معمر به، وعزاه السيوطي في الدر المنثور 6/ 323 إلى عبد بن حميد وابن المنذر.

notes.en: Abu Hayyan mentioned it in al-Bahr al-Muhit (8/437), as did Ibn Kathir in his Tafsir (8/367).
notes.ar: ذكره أبو حيان في البحر المحيط 8/ 437، وابن كثير في تفسيره 8/ 367.

notes.en: This is the reading of Nafiʿ, ʿAsim, Hamza, al-Kisaʾi, Ibn ʿAmir, Abu Jaʿfar al-Madani, and Khalaf. See al-Nashr (2/298).
notes.ar: وهى قراءة نافع وعاصم وحمزة والكسائي وابن عامر وأبى جعفر المدنى وخلف. النشر 2/ 298.

notes.en: This is the reading of Ibn Kathir, Abu ʿAmr, and Yaʿqub al-Hadrami. See al-Nashr (2/298).
notes.ar: وهى قراءة ابن كثير وأبي عمرو ويعقوب الحضرمي. النشر 2/ 298.

notes.en: See al-Farraʾ, Maʿani al-Qurʾan (3/245).
notes.ar: ينظر معاني القرآن للفراء 3/ 245.

notes.en: This is al-Nabigha; the source references were given earlier at 9/141.
notes.ar: هو النابغة، وقد تقدم تخريجه في 9/ 141.
